name: Lesotho
summary: A mountain kingdom completely surrounded by South Africa, founded by Moshoeshoe I in the 1820s; independent from Britain in 1966.

knownFor.label: Mokorotlo hat
knownFor.note: Conical straw hat on the flag.

location.value: Southern Africa, entirely surrounded by South Africa; about 30,355 km².

terrain.value: High mountains: the whole country is above 1,000 m, and over 80% lies above 1,800 m.

climate.value: Cool highland climate with warm wet summers (October–April) and cold dry winters; snow falls on the mountains and frost is common.

resources.value: Water from the Maloti Mountains, sold to South Africa, diamonds from mines such as Letšeng, and grazing land for sheep and goats.

disasters.value: Droughts that ruin harvests (such as in 2015–16), heavy snowfalls, and soil erosion that cuts deep gullies (dongas) in the lowlands.

population.value: About 2.1 million (2024 estimate, infobox); the article also gives about 2.28 million with no year.

urbanisation.value: About a third of the people live in towns; the capital Maseru is by far the largest, followed by Teyateyaneng and Mafeteng.

disease.value: One of the world’s highest HIV rates, affecting about a fifth of adults, along with tuberculosis.

migration.value: For decades many men worked in South African gold mines; since the 1990s mining jobs have fallen and more women migrate for work.

economicBase.value: Water from the Lesotho Highlands Water Project earned about US$70 million in 2010; Lesotho is the largest sub-Saharan exporter of garments to the US; the economy depends on remittances and Southern African Customs Union receipts, and the loti is at par with the rand.

tradeRoutes.value: The Lesotho Highlands Water Project, a 21-year multibillion-dollar scheme that began in 1986.

wealth.value: A lower-middle-income country by World Bank measures, with much rural poverty.

moneyAndTax.value: The loti (plural maloti), introduced in 1980 and tied one-to-one to the South African rand; customs union revenue is a major income.

inequality.value: Large gaps between the capital and rural areas.

governmentType.value: A parliamentary constitutional monarchy with a ceremonial king.

keyRulers.value: Moshoeshoe I formed Basutoland in 1822 (the lead says 1824). Moshoeshoe II was exiled in 1987 or 1990 (the page conflicts), reinstated in 1995 and died in 1996. Later and present leaders are not named here.

succession.value: The king is chosen from the royal family by the College of Chiefs; governments are formed after elections to the National Assembly.

institutions.value: A two-chamber Parliament: an elected National Assembly and a Senate of principal chiefs and nominated members; also the College of Chiefs.

stability.value: Political crisis and South African intervention (1998).

eliteConflict.value: Competition between political parties and leaders.

armyAndTech.value: The Lesotho Defence Force, a small army of about 2,000 soldiers, which has at times been drawn into politics.

majorWars.value: The 1998 crisis: South African and SADC forces intervened; the SADC forces withdrew in May 1999.

territoryChange.value: No changes since 1966; its borders were set in the 1860s, after much Basotho land was lost to the Orange Free State.

alliancesRivals.value: Member of the Southern African Development Community (SADC), the Southern African Customs Union and the Commonwealth; closely tied to South Africa.

inventions.value: No major inventions are associated with the modern state.

scienceEducation.value: The National University of Lesotho at Roma (begun in 1945 as Pius XII College); literacy is high for the region, especially among women.

openness.value: Open to trade and foreign investment, with periods of restriction.

communicationTransport.value: Mountain roads and passes such as Sani Pass, small airstrips and a short rail link from Maseru into South Africa; ponies are used in the highlands.

religion.value: Christian 92.1% (2020, infobox); the text says more than 95% (2011).

languageWriting.value: Sesotho, spoken by almost everyone and written since French missionaries arrived in the 1830s, and English; both are official.

artsArchitecture.value: Basotho blankets and the conical mokorotlo hat (shown on the flag), painted litema house walls, and San rock art in the mountains.

socialStructure.value: Almost everyone is Basotho; chiefs still allocate land in villages, alongside a small urban middle class.

sharedIdentity.value: A strong Basotho identity rooted in Moshoeshoe I, the Sesotho language, the monarchy and the mountains.

dailyLife.value: Many rural families live in stone or mud-brick rondavels, grow maize and keep animals, and eat papa (maize porridge) with vegetables.

neighbours.value: Completely surrounded by South Africa: its Free State, KwaZulu-Natal and Eastern Cape provinces.

ideasReligions.value: Christian missions, beginning with French Protestants at Morija (1833), shaped schooling, writing and religion.

colonisation.value: A British protectorate (Basutoland) from 1868; independent from the UK on 4 October 1966.

riseSignals.value: The Basotho polity was formed under King Moshoeshoe I (the article gives 1822 and 1824); independence on 4 October 1966.

peakPeriod.value: Too recent to judge; the Highlands Water Project (from 1986) became a major source of income.

declineSignals.value: None that define the country as a whole.

outcome.value: Still an independent kingdom, and a member of the UN and the Commonwealth since 1966.

overallCertainty.value: Basic facts are well documented; some figures are estimates.
